chosen.premise: Parasect is mostly dead: its mushroom is the main body, and removing it stops the bug from moving.
chosen.hook: Parasect may not be the bug you think it is.
chosen.visualIdea: Show the mushroom growing over the bug, then cut to the host freezing when the mushroom disappears.
chosen.note: A highly Parasect-specific identity reversal, directly supported by multiple entries: the mushroom is the main body, controls the Pokémon, and the bug stops moving without it.

candidates.premise: When Parasect’s mushroom has extracted everything from the bug, it leaves spores on the bug’s egg.
candidates.hook: The mushroom doesn’t stop when Parasect runs out of energy.
candidates.visualIdea: Follow clues from drained energy to an empty host, then reveal spores being left on an egg.
candidates.note: Extremely specific, disturbing, and visually strong. The egg detail is directly supported, though the premise should carefully distinguish the mushroom from Parasect itself.

candidates.premise: Parasect infest large trees en masse, and when one dies, they all move to another tree together.
candidates.hook: When their tree dies, Parasect relocate as one swarm.
candidates.visualIdea: Animate Parasect draining a tree’s roots, then swarm across the forest to the next trunk.
candidates.note: A clear ecological behavior with strong animation potential and excellent evidence, but it feels more like a species behavior than Parasect’s most shocking identity hook.

candidates.premise: Parasect’s toxic spores are poisonous, yet people also harvest them to make herbal medicine.
candidates.hook: Parasect’s poison can also become medicine.
candidates.visualIdea: Split the screen between a toxic spore cloud and the same spores being boiled into a medicinal brew.
candidates.note: The poisonous-spore versus medicine contradiction is compelling and well supported, though the broader poison-to-medicine premise could fit other fictional organisms.

candidates.premise: Parasect stays in dark, damp places not because the bug prefers them, but because the mushroom does.
candidates.hook: Parasect’s favorite habitat belongs to the mushroom, not the bug.
candidates.visualIdea: Show the bug resisting a damp cave while the mushroom pulls Parasect deeper into darkness.
candidates.note: The mushroom-versus-host habitat distinction is specific and supported, but the visual conflict and reveal are less powerful than the control premise.

candidates.premise: The larger Parasect’s mushroom grows, the stronger the spores it scatters become.
candidates.hook: For Parasect, a bigger mushroom means a stronger weapon.
candidates.visualIdea: Scale up the mushroom cap while spore clouds intensify from weak to poisonous.
candidates.note: The growth-to-spore-strength rule is concrete and well supported, but less surprising and less distinctive than the control reveal. “Weapon” is slightly interpretive.
